title: Backend TypeScript Sources and the JavaScript They Become
hints: TypeScript source lives in Build/Sources/TypeScript/ and the JavaScript generated from it in the owning system extension's Resources/Public/JavaScript/. The generated file is committed, so a source change that is not built leaves the two disagreeing and the browser running the old one.
This is the core's asset pipeline. A project extension owns a separate build; see extension-asset-build.

hints.text: A label bundle a module imports as ~labels/<domain> is not one of these generated files. It is an HTTP response the backend builds per request, so no build invalidates it and no rebuild fixes it — javascript-labels says what does.

hints: Keep TypeScript source and generated JavaScript in sync.
Prefer existing TYPO3 backend imports, event patterns, and custom element conventions used nearby.

Build/eslint.config.mjs decides the style, and CI=true ./Build/Scripts/runTests.sh -s lintTypescript settles a question about it. That file is the list: what it does not configure is untidiness rather than a lint failure.

@typescript-eslint/member-ordering is enforced, so where a member sits in a class is checked rather than left to taste, and adding a static method is where that lands. @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any and @typescript-eslint/no-inferrable-types are off on purpose, so neither is a finding — imitating a neighbouring file turns a rule that is switched off into a diff nobody asked for.

hints.text: jQuery is reached through an import, import $ from 'jquery', and the bare globals $ and jQuery are refused with that import as the message. The restriction is why a file cannot pick the global up from the page the way a script tag once did.
jQuery is not a core dependency: Build/package.json does not list it and the lint config carries no restriction on it, because there is nothing left to restrict.

hints: Frontend modules with state transitions should have focused JavaScript unit coverage.

title: Async Data in a Backend Web Component and How Its Failure Shows
appliesTo: async data in a web component
hints: A backend web component loads data through a Task from @lit/task and renders it with task.render(), which takes one branch per state: pending while it runs, complete with the value, error with the reason it rejected.

The error branch renders only where the task function rejects. A task that catches its own failure and returns an empty value renders complete instead, so the branch the component declares is unreachable and the failure reaches the user as an empty result.
So a failure is surfaced by letting the task reject, and the declared branch renders it. A second error surface written beside that branch duplicates one the component already has and cannot reach.

title: Backend UI and Web Components
hints: Keep custom elements focused on rendering and interaction orchestration.
Keep state transitions explicit and testable.
Check accessibility behavior for controls, dialogs, drag and drop, and status indicators.
For custom elements, keep CSS aligned with the host element API, stable attributes, slots, parts, and custom properties.

A custom element's constructor takes no parameters, which wc/no-constructor-params enforces and the browser imposes anyway: it constructs the element with none. What the element needs arrives as an attribute, a property or a slot.

A listener a component adds is removed again, which wc/require-listener-teardown enforces. The one that leaks is the listener on something outliving the element - document, window, or another element - because the element is torn down and the listener is not.
